publishedEducationalOperatingTableSectio: Course Schedule: Online Lecture & In-Class Workshop Thursdays 12:00-13:15 PM Location: 수선관 61801 Office Hours: schedule via email Teaching Assistant: TBD Course Description and Objectives This course introduces students to core methodological concepts and strategies used in social science research, including research design, sampling and measurement, experimental research, survey research, ethnographic research, interview-based research, and content analysis. Throughout the semester we will develop the analytical skills necessary to interrogate epistemological assumptions in published social science research specifically and truth-claims generally. In addition to critically evaluating previous research, students will collect and analyze data based on the different methods discussed in class. By the end of the course, students should have acquired valuable research skills widely applicable in academic and professional settings. Each week is organized into two complementary parts. Earlier in the week, students attend an online lecture (uploaded on Canvas) that introduces the week's methodological concepts, key readings, and analytical frameworks. On Thursdays, students meet in class for discussion and hands-on practice, examining the week's required readings and applying course concepts through in-class exercises. At the end of this course, students will be able to: 1. Understand the theoretical bases and ethical considerations of social science research. 2. Articulate key components of the various research methods used by sociologists, including: survey research, experimental research, ethnographic research, interview-based research, content analysis, and historical/archival research. 3. Identify the strengths and weaknesses of these methodological approaches. 4. Match appropriate research methods with research questions. 5. Critically evaluate existing social science research. 6. Design and carry out empirical research protocols. Course Requirements *Depending on the number of enrolled students, assignment details are subject to change All major assignments, with the exception of the Final Research Proposal, are due at 11:59pm on Sundays. Each due date is noted below. Details of the assignment will be presented as the course progresses. Research Design Assignment 30% Students of methodology should be able to conceive of (or "propose") their own research projects after completing this course. This assessment looks for the ability to design a project with a clear link between the research question and method, that demonstrates understanding of foundational concepts, that adheres to method-specific protocols, and that engages with 2 relevant ethical considerations. This portion of the course will be assessed via a series of assignments that take students from an initial idea to a complete research proposal. 1. Preliminary Research Proposal 5%: This assignment is the first step in our semester-long project of developing a research proposal. It requires students to identify a question of interest, consider how it could be answered via social science research, and engage with relevant literature. (due October 4 11:59 pm) 2. Final Research Proposal 25%: This final assignment is an opportunity to comprehensively apply what students have learned throughout the semester in constructing a complete research design. (due December 15 11:59pm) Practice Assignments 50% Because social science research relies on data, students will practice the skill of data collection. Students will gain experience obtaining data from people and from observations. The assignments in this portion of the course require students to demonstrate understanding of the relevant standards and considerations presented in class and readings. 1. Interview practice 25% (due October 25 11:59 pm) 2. Observation practice 25% (due November 22 11:59 pm) Class Attendance and Participation 20% As half of the course is composed of discussion and activities, participation in class discussions and in-class exercises is essential. You must arrive at the Thursday class having watched that week's online lecture, prepared to discuss the required readings and to take part in the in-class exercise. Groups will be assigned at the start of the semester and may be reorganized at midterm. For most in-class activities you will work in your assigned group, but participation is assessed individually: at the end of most Thursday sessions, you will submit an in-class exercise submission through Canvas. Missing more than 1 required class (including both online and offline meetings) will lead to deductions, as will little or no participation. Thursday In-Class Exercise Submissions: Most Thursday sessions include a hands-on exercise—for example, drafting interview questions, building a coding scheme, or designing an experiment. At the end of these sessions, each student submits the product of that day's work through the Assignment tab on Canvas. The specific deliverable varies by week and will be announced in class; it may be a brief written reflection or a more developed document such as a questionnaire or a research design. Although much of the in-class work is done in assigned groups, every student submits individually. Submissions are due shortly after each class and are graded for completion. Readings We will read both a standard methods textbook and a collection of other scholarly pieces. The textbook should be approached as an introduction to our class discussions and a reference manual. The other pieces, from sociological research journals and monographs, demonstrate the concepts and methodologies we cover. There will be some overlap between lecture and reading material, but we won’t cover all reading material in class and vice versa. All readings except for Babbie’s textbook are available on Canvas. 3 Textbook: Earl Babbie’s The Practice of Social Research.15th edition. A physical copy is on reserve at 중앙학술정보관. It is also available for purchase via vendors like 알라딘 and 교보문고. Course Policies 1. Communication Please contact the instructor and teaching assistant(s) by email, not through Canvas messaging. We aim to respond within 24-48 hours on weekdays; don’t expect replies over weekends and holidays. Please plan accordingly and avoid sending time-sensitive questions at the last minute. When you write, please include the course number (USS 2001) in the subject line. For matters easier to discuss in person, please arrange a time for office hours. 2. Preparing the Readings Reading the assigned material closely and on time is essential to following the course and participating well. Because this is a methods course, read each empirical study as a researcher, not only for its conclusions. For every research article, come prepared to answer: • What data and methods did the author use? • What is the central argument or claim? • What evidence supports that claim, and how convincing is it? • What are the study's limitations? • How does this reading connect to the week's methodological theme? Bringing notes on these questions will make our Thursday discussions and your assignments noticeably stronger. 3. Class Participation and Discussion Watching the lecture and reading the assigned materials before class is what makes full participation in discussion and activities possible. In discussion, focus on the quality of your reasoning rather than the quantity of your comments. You are not expected to arrive with polished answers—you are expected to think out loud, test ideas against the evidence, and engage seriously with the readings and with one another. If something in a reading is unclear to you, it is very likely unclear to others too; raising it helps the whole class. Several Thursday sessions involve debate and structured disagreement, so please engage your classmates' ideas critically but respectfully. 4. Submitting Assignments Major assignments are submitted on Canvas as Word documents (.docx) by the stated deadline. Late submissions are penalized 5% per day late. If a serious illness or unavoidable circumstance arises, contact the instructor before the deadline to discuss options. Thursday in-class exercise write-ups must also be submitted on Canvas as Word documents; failure to submit a write-up as required will affect your participation grade. 5. Technology in the Classroom Technology in class is a double-edged sword: it can help, but it can also be a major distraction. During lecture and discussion, please use laptops and tablets for note-taking and coursework only, and close web browsers, email, and messaging so you can stay focused. I trust your autonomy here; let's protect a focused, shared learning environment together. On Thursdays, bring a laptop or tablet so you can complete and submit the in-class exercise on Canvas before you leave. 4 6. Academic Integrity and Independent Work All submitted work must be your own. Cite every source you draw on using ASA style (ASA Quick Style Guide). Plagiarism—presenting another person's words or ideas as your own, or reusing your own prior work without acknowledgment—is grounds for failing the assignment or the course and may be referred for disciplinary action. Research integrity. Because this course trains you to produce empirical evidence, the standards that govern professional research apply to your assignments as well: you may not fabricate or falsify data, fieldnotes, codes, or results. Inventing or altering data is a serious violation of research ethics, not a shortcut—and it is precisely the standard this course teaches you to uphold. 7. Use of Generative AI In this course, the use of generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and similar tools) is not permitted, except as a translation aid for English-language readings (see below). Why this policy. The goal of this course is not to produce assignments as finished products, but to build skills you can only develop by doing the work yourself: reading scholarly and empirical texts critically, formulating your own research questions, designing studies, working directly with data, and writing up what you find in your own words. These are the core competencies of a social scientist, and they are built through the effort of thinking— effort that disappears when a tool does the work for you. This view is widely shared among educators who study AI and learning. Dan Levy of the Harvard Kennedy School, co-author of Teaching Effectively with ChatGPT, argues that "no learning occurs unless the brain is actively engaged in making meaning"—ask a tool for the answer, and that active engagement, along with the learning that depends on it, never takes place. Karen Thornber, Faculty Director of Harvard's Derek Bok Center for Teaching and Learning, offers a navigation analogy: just as relying on turn-by-turn GPS leaves us knowing our own city's streets far less well than the cities we learned before GPS, over-relying on AI can cost us the chance to develop certain mental skills in the first place. And as the philosopher Jeff Behrends notes, the tools we use while thinking shape how we think—much as taking notes by hand produces better recall than typing them. Leaning on AI to generate polished output without going through the underlying reasoning yields surface results while quietly undermining your long-term intellectual growth. The aim is not to reject these tools forever. Once you have built strong foundations in critical thinking, analysis, and writing as an undergraduate, you will be far better positioned to use AI well — as a genuine tool rather than a substitute for your own judgment. For a fuller discussion, see the Harvard Gazette, "Is AI Dulling Our Minds?" (November 13, 2025): https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2025/11/is-ai-dulling-our-minds/ Permitted use. You may use AI translation tools to help you understand academic texts written in English. Because automated translation can introduce errors and subtle distortions, the English original always governs—use translation as a support, not a replacement for reading the source. Prohibited uses include, but are not limited to: 5 • Writing, drafting, outlining, or revising the substance of any assignment, including your research proposal • Generating research questions, hypotheses, arguments, or ideas • Designing research instruments (interview guides, questionnaires, observation protocols, codebooks) • Fabricating, completing, or "filling in" data of any kind—interview guides, fieldnotes, survey responses, codes, or analytic results (in a methods course this is doubly serious: both academic dishonesty and a research-integrity violation) • Analyzing or coding your data on your behalf • Searching for, selecting, or summarizing sources, or conducting your literature review • Summarizing or analyzing assigned readings Suspected or confirmed use of AI outside the permitted exception will be treated as a violation of academic integrity and may result in a zero on the assignment or failure of the course. 8. Research Ethics with Human Participants This course requires you to conduct your own interviews and observations. All research you carry out for the course must follow the ethical principles we cover in class: voluntary informed consent, the participant's right to decline or withdraw at any time, confidentiality and secure handling of any information you collect, anonymization of identifying details in your write-ups, and the obligation to avoid harm. Do not collect sensitive personal information, and do not recruit vulnerable participants, without discussing it with the instructor first. If you are unsure whether something is appropriate, ask before you collect any data. 9. Accessibility and Learning Support Students who need accommodations for a disability or health condition should notify the instructor within the first two weeks of the semester so we can arrange appropriate support, and contact SKKU Support Center for Students with Disabilities as needed. This portion of the course will be assessed via a series of assignments that take students from an initial idea to a complete research proposal. 1. Preliminary Research Proposal 5%: This assignment is the first step in our semester-long project of developing a research proposal. It requires students to identify a question of interest, consider how it could be answered via social science research, and engage with relevant literature. (due October 4 11:59 pm) 2. Final Research Proposal 25%: This final assignment is an opportunity to comprehensively apply what students have learned throughout the semester in constructing a complete research design. (due December 15 11:59pm) Practice Assignments 50% Because social science research relies on data, students will practice the skill of data collection. Students will gain experience obtaining data from people and from observations. The assignments in this portion of the course require students to demonstrate understanding of the relevant standards and considerations presented in class and readings. 1. Interview practice 25% (due October 25 11:59 pm) 2. Observation practice 25% (due November 22 11:59 pm) Class Attendance and Participation 20% As half of the course is composed of discussion and activities, participation in class discussions and in-class exercises is essential. You must arrive at the Thursday class having watched that week's online lecture, prepared to discuss the required readings and to take part in the in-class exercise. Groups will be assigned at the start of the semester and may be reorganized at midterm. For most in-class activities you will work in your assigned group, but participation is assessed individually: at the end of most Thursday sessions, you will submit an in-class exercise submission through Canvas. Missing more than 1 required class (including both online and offline meetings) will lead to deductions, as will little or no participation. Thursday In-Class Exercise Submissions: Most Thursday sessions include a hands-on exercise—for example, drafting interview questions, building a coding scheme, or designing an experiment. At the end of these sessions, each student submits the product of that day's work through the Assignment tab on Canvas. The specific deliverable varies by week and will be announced in class; it may be a brief written reflection or a more developed document such as a questionnaire or a research design. Although much of the in-class work is done in assigned groups, every student submits individually. Submissions are due shortly after each class and are graded for completion. Readings We will read both a standard methods textbook and a collection of other scholarly pieces. The textbook should be approached as an introduction to our class discussions and a reference manual. The other pieces, from sociological research journals and monographs, demonstrate the concepts and methodologies we cover. There will be some overlap between lecture and reading material, but we won’t cover all reading material in class and vice versa. All readings except for Babbie’s textbook are available on Canvas. 3 Textbook: Earl Babbie’s The Practice of Social Research.15th edition. A physical copy is on reserve at 중앙학술정보관. It is also available for purchase via vendors like 알라딘 and 교보문고. Course Policies 1. Communication Please contact the instructor and teaching assistant(s) by email, not through Canvas messaging. We aim to respond within 24-48 hours on weekdays; don’t expect replies over weekends and holidays. Please plan accordingly and avoid sending time-sensitive questions at the last minute. When you write, please include the course number (USS 2001) in the subject line. For matters easier to discuss in person, please arrange a time for office hours. 2. Preparing the Readings Reading the assigned material closely and on time is essential to following the course and participating well. Because this is a methods course, read each empirical study as a researcher, not only for its conclusions. For every research article, come prepared to answer: • What data and methods did the author use? • What is the central argument or claim? • What evidence supports that claim, and how convincing is it? • What are the study's limitations? • How does this reading connect to the week's methodological theme? Bringing notes on these questions will make our Thursday discussions and your assignments noticeably stronger. 3. Class Participation and Discussion Watching the lecture and reading the assigned materials before class is what makes full participation in discussion and activities possible. In discussion, focus on the quality of your reasoning rather than the quantity of your comments. You are not expected to arrive with polished answers—you are expected to think out loud, test ideas against the evidence, and engage seriously with the readings and with one another. If something in a reading is unclear to you, it is very likely unclear to others too; raising it helps the whole class. Several Thursday sessions involve debate and structured disagreement, so please engage your classmates' ideas critically but respectfully. 4. During lecture and discussion, please use laptops and tablets for note-taking and coursework only, and close web browsers, email, and messaging so you can stay focused. I trust your autonomy here; let's protect a focused, shared learning environment together. On Thursdays, bring a laptop or tablet so you can complete and submit the in-class exercise on Canvas before you leave. 4 6. Academic Integrity and Independent Work All submitted work must be your own. Cite every source you draw on using ASA style (ASA Quick Style Guide). Plagiarism—presenting another person's words or ideas as your own, or reusing your own prior work without acknowledgment—is grounds for failing the assignment or the course and may be referred for disciplinary action. Research integrity. Because this course trains you to produce empirical evidence, the standards that govern professional research apply to your assignments as well: you may not fabricate or falsify data, fieldnotes, codes, or results. Inventing or altering data is a serious violation of research ethics, not a shortcut—and it is precisely the standard this course teaches you to uphold. 7. Use of Generative AI In this course, the use of generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and similar tools) is not permitted, except as a translation aid for English-language readings (see below). Why this policy. The goal of this course is not to produce assignments as finished products, but to build skills you can only develop by doing the work yourself: reading scholarly and empirical texts critically, formulating your own research questions, designing studies, working directly with data, and writing up what you find in your own words. These are the core competencies of a social scientist, and they are built through the effort of thinking— effort that disappears when a tool does the work for you. This view is widely shared among educators who study AI and learning. Dan Levy of the Harvard Kennedy School, co-author of Teaching Effectively with ChatGPT, argues that "no learning occurs unless the brain is actively engaged in making meaning"—ask a tool for the answer, and that active engagement, along with the learning that depends on it, never takes place. Karen Thornber, Faculty Director of Harvard's Derek Bok Center for Teaching and Learning, offers a navigation analogy: just as relying on turn-by-turn GPS leaves us knowing our own city's streets far less well than the cities we learned before GPS, over-relying on AI can cost us the chance to develop certain mental skills in the first place. And as the philosopher Jeff Behrends notes, the tools we use while thinking shape how we think—much as taking notes by hand produces better recall than typing them. Leaning on AI to generate polished output without going through the underlying reasoning yields surface results while quietly undermining your long-term intellectual growth. The aim is not to reject these tools forever. Once you have built strong foundations in critical thinking, analysis, and writing as an undergraduate, you will be far better positioned to use AI well — as a genuine tool rather than a substitute for your own judgment. For a fuller discussion, see the Harvard Gazette, "Is AI Dulling Our Minds?" (November 13, 2025): https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2025/11/is-ai-dulling-our-minds/ Permitted use. You may use AI translation tools to help you understand academic texts written in English. Because automated translation can introduce errors and subtle distortions, the English original always governs—use translation as a support, not a replacement for reading the source. Prohibited uses include, but are not limited to: 5 • Writing, drafting, outlining, or revising the substance of any assignment, including your research proposal • Generating research questions, hypotheses, arguments, or ideas • Designing research instruments (interview guides, questionnaires, observation protocols, codebooks) • Fabricating, completing, or "filling in" data of any kind—interview guides, fieldnotes, survey responses, codes, or analytic results (in a methods course this is doubly serious: both academic dishonesty and a research-integrity violation) • Analyzing or coding your data on your behalf • Searching for, selecting, or summarizing sources, or conducting your literature review • Summarizing or analyzing assigned readings Suspected or confirmed use of AI outside the permitted exception will be treated as a violation of academic integrity and may result in a zero on the assignment or failure of the course. 8. Research Ethics with Human Participants This course requires you to conduct your own interviews and observations. All research you carry out for the course must follow the ethical principles we cover in class: voluntary informed consent, the participant's right to decline or withdraw at any time, confidentiality and secure handling of any information you collect, anonymization of identifying details in your write-ups, and the obligation to avoid harm. Do not collect sensitive personal information, and do not recruit vulnerable participants, without discussing it with the instructor first. If you are unsure whether something is appropriate, ask before you collect any data. 9. The Elements of Journalism 이재경 옮김, 『저널리즘의 기본원칙』, 한국언론진흥재단. 토론 질문: 객관 보도와 해석 저널리즘 중 어느 것이 시민에게 더 책임 있는 보도 방식일까? 언론의 역할은 사실 전달만으로 충분한가, 아니면 해석과 맥락 제공까지 해야 하는가? 선거 보도에서 정치인의 거짓말을 언론은 중립적으로 단순 보도해야 하는가, 아니면 국민의 알권리를 위해서 적극적으로 검증해야 하는가? BBC, NYT, 한국기자협회 등의 윤리강령 및 실천요강은 무엇인가? 어떤 공통점과 차이점이 있는가? 4주차(9/24) 이해의 상충(conflicts of interest) - 광고와 윤리 (추석연휴 보강: 온라인 녹화 강의) 사전 학습: 산업적 논리와 저널리즘의 사회적 책임 간 상충, 기사형(허위, 과장, 간접) 광고의 문제 토론 질문: 광고는 소비자의 선택권을 해치고 있는가, 아니면 자유를 확장하는가? 만일 광고가 소비자의 자유를 해친다면, 그 방식은 무엇인가? 공익광고와 상업광고를 구분하는 기준은 무엇인가? 그 경계를 어떻게 설정할 수 있을까? 5주차(10/1) 프라이버시와 미디어 윤리 사전 학습: 국민의 알 권리, 알 필요성, 알기 원하는 것 간의 분별력 키우기, 롤스의 ‘무지의 장막’ 이해 생각해 볼 사례 – 한국 탐사보도 기사 (예: 뉴스타파, KBS⋅MBC⋅JTBC 심층 보도) 토론 질문: 공익적 탐사보도를 위해 개인의 사생활 침해는 정당화될 수 있는가? 실제 한국 사례 중 윤리적 판단이 모호했던 사건은 무엇이며, 어떻게 평가할 수 있을까? 최근 한국 언론의 탐사보도 사례에서 윤리적 과오와 정당성을 어떻게 평가할 수 있을까?) 6주차(10/8) 미디어의 젠더⋅사회소수자 재현 사전 학습: 미디어에서 젠더·인종·사회소수자 등이 재현되는가, 어떻게 재현되는가는 왜 중요한가? 과소 재현되거나 부정적으로 재현돼 논란이 된 광고/드라마 장면들은 무엇인가? 이러한 재현이 왜 문제가 되는가? 토론 질문: 소수자 재현은 ‘존재’ 자체가 중요한가, 아니면 ‘어떻게’ 재현되는가가 중요한가? 젠더 감수성 결여 보도가 사회에 끼치는 장기적 영향은 무엇일까? 7주차(10/15) 포토저널리즘과 윤리 사전 학습: 보도사진의 프레이밍 효과, 죽음 관련 보도사진의 취재윤리, 초상권, 사진 조작 및 합성 토론 질문: 실제 보도사진(영상) 사례를 골라 이 사진의 윤리적 측면, 프레이밍 효과와 메시지에 대해 분석·토론하고 그 함의를 찾아본다. 8주차(10/22) 중간고사 (범위 – 7주차 강의까지) 9주차(10/29) 뉴스 리터러시 사전 학습: 허위조작정보(fake news, disinformation)와 팩트 체킹(fact-checking) 사례 조사: 국내외 팩트체크 기사 1~2편 토론 질문: 가짜뉴스 규제는 표현의 자유 침해인가, 민주주의 수호인가? AI 생성 콘텐츠(뉴스, 이미지 등)를 시민이 구분할 수 없을 때 교육과 규제 중 무엇이 더 효과적일까? 10주차(11/5) 개인방송(유튜브 등)과 디지털 영상 콘텐츠의 윤리와 리터러시 사전 학습: 혐오 발언(hate speech), 사이버 렉카, 디지털 성폭력(딥페이크 등)의 문제 토론 질문: 비윤리적·폭력적인 디지털 영상 콘텐츠의 유통과 소비를 막을 수 있는 방안은? 호주(16세 미만), 프랑스(15세 미만)에서는 미성년자의 SNS 사용 금지 법안을 통과시켰다. 최근 국내에서도 14세 미만 청소년의 SNS 가입 금지 법안을 추진중에 있다. 이에 대한 여러분의 생각은? 11주차(11/12) AI 윤리와 리터러시 사전 학습: 알고리즘 편향(Algorithm bias)과 불평등의 문제, 개인정보 보호 등 관련 영상 시청 토론 질문: 플랫폼 기업은 이용자 데이터 보호보다 혁신을 우선할 권리가 있는가? 알고리즘 편향은 기술적 문제인가, 아니면 윤리적 책임의 문제인가? 알고리즘(AI 기반) 추천 시스템은 단순한 기술적 도구인가, 사회적 책임을 져야 하는가? ※12~14주차 팀발표. 조편성 및 발표와 관련된 세부 사항은 수강 인원 확정 후 공지 예정. 발표 주제 및 내용 – 팀별로 뉴스, 딥페이크, AI 아나운서, 혐오표현 등 한 가지 주제를 골라 그에 해당하는 사례를 조사. 사례의 윤리적 문제와 대안을 제시. 즉, 사례에서 드러난 윤리적 딜레마는 무엇인가? 우리가 생각해볼 수 있는 사회문화적⋅정책적 대안은 무엇인가? 발표 방식: 사전 발표 영상물 제작 & 제출 – 사전에 발표를 촬영한 영상물을 팀당 1명이 대표로 아이캠퍼스 토론란으로 제출함 오프라인 대면 수업 – 학생들은 조별 발표물을 미리 시청한 후 관련 질문이나 제언을 준비해 와 Q&A에 참여함. 발표팀은 예상 질문에 대한 답변을 준비해와야 함. 12주(11/19) 팀발표 및 질의응답 I 13주(11/26) 팀발표 및 질의응답 II 14주(12/3) 팀발표 및 질의응답 III 15주(12/10) 기말고사 및 종강 氠瑢 과제물 주차별 수업내용 참조

Media Literacies”, Media Education: Literacy, Learning and Contemporary Culture, Polity Press.§토론 질문: 아래 토론 질문은 변경될 수 있음-미디어 윤리, 미디어 리터러시란 무엇인가? 미디어 윤리와 미디어 리터러시는 어떤 접점에서 만나는가? -미디어 리터러시는 단순 정보 활용 능력인가, 민주적 참여 능력인가? -미디어 교육은 가치 중립적이어야 할까, 아니면 비판적 가치를 지향해야 할까? 2주차(9/10) 미디어 윤리의 철학적 원칙과 모델 §사전 학습: 철학적 윤리 이론 (아리스토텔레스의 최상의 중용, 칸트의 정언명령, 벤담과 밀의 공리주의 등)과 윤리적 판단 모델 (포터 박스와 보크 모델) §생각해볼 문제 – 공리주의와 칸트 윤리는 동일한 미디어 사건(예: 연예인 스캔들 보도)에 대해 어떤 상반된 결론을 내릴까?3주차(9/17) 저널리즘의 윤리학§사전 학습: 진실 추구, 이상적 저널리즘으로서의 객관적 보도 vs 해석적 저널리즘, 저널리즘(저널리스트)의 역할과 책임, 자율규제로서의 언론윤리강령과 실천 요강v참고자료: Kovach, B., & Rosenstiel, T. (2021). The Elements of Journalism 이재경 옮김, 『저널리즘의 기본원칙』, 한국언론진흥재단. §토론 질문: -객관 보도와 해석 저널리즘 중 어느 것이 시민에게 더 책임 있는 보도 방식일까?-언론의 역할은 사실 전달만으로 충분한가, 아니면 해석과 맥락 제공까지 해야 하는가? -선거 보도에서 정치인의 거짓말을 언론은 중립적으로 단순 보도해야 하는가, 아니면 국민의 알권리를 위해서 적극적으로 검증해야 하는가?-BBC, NYT, 한국기자협회 등의 윤리강령 및 실천요강은 무엇인가? 어떤 공통점과 차이점이 있는가?4주차(9/24) 이해의 상충(conflicts of interest) - 광고와 윤리 (추석연휴 보강: 온라인 녹화 강의)§사전 학습: 산업적 논리와 저널리즘의 사회적 책임 간 상충, 기사형(허위, 과장, 간접) 광고의 문제 §토론 질문: -광고는 소비자의 선택권을 해치고 있는가, 아니면 자유를 확장하는가? 만일 광고가 소비자의 자유를 해친다면, 그 방식은 무엇인가? -공익광고와 상업광고를 구분하는 기준은 무엇인가? 그 경계를 어떻게 설정할 수 있을까?5주차(10/1) 프라이버시와 미디어 윤리 §사전 학습: 국민의 알 권리, 알 필요성, 알기 원하는 것 간의 분별력 키우기, 롤스의 ‘무지의 장막’ 이해v생각해 볼 사례 – 한국 탐사보도 기사 (예: 뉴스타파, KBS⋅MBC⋅JTBC 심층 보도) - 3 - §토론 질문: -공익적 탐사보도를 위해 개인의 사생활 침해는 정당화될 수 있는가? -실제 한국 사례 중 윤리적 판단이 모호했던 사건은 무엇이며, 어떻게 평가할 수 있을까? -최근 한국 언론의 탐사보도 사례에서 윤리적 과오와 정당성을 어떻게 평가할 수 있을까?) 6주차(10/8) 미디어의 젠더⋅사회소수자 재현§사전 학습: 미디어에서 젠더·인종·사회소수자 등이 재현되는가, 어떻게 재현되는가는 왜 중요한가? 과소 재현되거나 부정적으로 재현돼 논란이 된 광고/드라마 장면들은 무엇인가? 이러한 재현이 왜 문제가 되는가? §토론 질문: -소수자 재현은 ‘존재’ 자체가 중요한가, 아니면 ‘어떻게’ 재현되는가가 중요한가? -젠더 감수성 결여 보도가 사회에 끼치는 장기적 영향은 무엇일까? 7주차(10/15) 포토저널리즘과 윤리 §사전 학습: 보도사진의 프레이밍 효과, 죽음 관련 보도사진의 취재윤리, 초상권, 사진 조작 및 합성§토론 질문: -실제 보도사진(영상) 사례를 골라 이 사진의 윤리적 측면, 프레이밍 효과와 메시지에 대해 분석·토론하고 그 함의를 찾아본다.8주차(10/22) 중간고사 (범위 – 7주차 강의까지)9주차(10/29) 뉴스 리터러시 §사전 학습: 허위조작정보(fake news, disinformation)와 팩트 체킹(fact-checking)v사례 조사: 국내외 팩트체크 기사 1~2편§토론 질문: -가짜뉴스 규제는 표현의 자유 침해인가, 민주주의 수호인가? -AI 생성 콘텐츠(뉴스, 이미지 등)를 시민이 구분할 수 없을 때 교육과 규제 중 무엇이 더 효과적일까?10주차(11/5) 개인방송(유튜브 등)과 디지털 영상 콘텐츠의 윤리와 리터러시 §사전 학습: 혐오 발언(hate speech), 사이버 렉카, 디지털 성폭력(딥페이크 등)의 문제§토론 질문: -비윤리적·폭력적인 디지털 영상 콘텐츠의 유통과 소비를 막을 수 있는 방안은?-호주(16세 미만), 프랑스(15세 미만)에서는 미성년자의 SNS 사용 금지 법안을 통과시켰다. 최근 국내에서도 14세 미만 청소년의 SNS 가입 금지 법안을 추진중에 있다. 이에 대한 여러분의 생각은? 11주차(11/12) AI 윤리와 리터러시 §사전 학습: 알고리즘 편향(Algorithm bias)과 불평등의 문제, 개인정보 보호 등 관련 영상 시청 - 4 - §토론 질문: -플랫폼 기업은 이용자 데이터 보호보다 혁신을 우선할 권리가 있는가? -알고리즘 편향은 기술적 문제인가, 아니면 윤리적 책임의 문제인가?-알고리즘(AI 기반) 추천 시스템은 단순한 기술적 도구인가, 사회적 책임을 져야 하는가? ※12~14주차 팀발표. 조편성 및 발표와 관련된 세부 사항은 수강 인원 확정 후 공지 예정. §발표 주제 및 내용 – 팀별로 뉴스, 딥페이크, AI 아나운서, 혐오표현 등 한 가지 주제를 골라 그에 해당하는 사례를 조사. 사례의 윤리적 문제와 대안을 제시. 즉, 사례에서 드러난 윤리적 딜레마는 무엇인가? 우리가 생각해볼 수 있는 사회문화적⋅정책적 대안은 무엇인가? §발표 방식:F사전 발표 영상물 제작 & 제출 – 사전에 발표를 촬영한 영상물을 팀당 1명이 대표로 아이캠퍼스 토론란으로 제출함 F오프라인 대면 수업 – 학생들은 조별 발표물을 미리 시청한 후 관련 질문이나 제언을 준비해 와 Q&A에 참여함. 발표팀은 예상 질문에 대한 답변을 준비해와야 함. 12주(11/19) 팀발표 및 질의응답 I13주(11/26) 팀발표 및 질의응답 II14주(12/3) 팀발표 및 질의응답 III15주(12/10) 기말고사 및 종강과제물주차별 수업내용 참조

-AI 생성 콘텐츠(뉴스, 이미지 등)를 시민이 구분할 수 없을 때 교육과 규제 중 무엇이 더 효과적일까?10주차(11/5) 개인방송(유튜브 등)과 디지털 영상 콘텐츠의 윤리와 리터러시 §사전 학습: 혐오 발언(hate speech), 사이버 렉카, 디지털 성폭력(딥페이크 등)의 문제§토론 질문: -비윤리적·폭력적인 디지털 영상 콘텐츠의 유통과 소비를 막을 수 있는 방안은?-호주(16세 미만), 프랑스(15세 미만)에서는 미성년자의 SNS 사용 금지 법안을 통과시켰다. 최근 국내에서도 14세 미만 청소년의 SNS 가입 금지 법안을 추진중에 있다. 이에 대한 여러분의 생각은? Weekly Assignments o Mondays (Online): Students are required to watch the online lectures and complete all scheduled weekly quizzes (13 sessions in total) and Figma tutorial follow -along assignments (conducted over 6 weeks). o Wednesdays (Offline): Active participation in and completion of weekly in -class activities is required. 2. Final Project o Project Deliverable: For the final project, you are required to submit a mid-fidelity mobile app prototype . This assignment focuses on structural integrity and user experience (UX) logic rather than high-end visual aesthetics. o Detailed Guidelines: o Focus on Structure over Visual Polish: High-resolution images or complex graphic effects are not mandatory. However, even with a minimal use of color and imagery, the positioning of elements and information hierarchy must be refined enough to feel like a professional, real -world service. o Reflect Brand Identity: The prototype should clearly convey the brand’s character and concept through its overall tone, manner, and design choices. o Use Real Content: The use of 'Lorem Ipsum' or placeholder text is strictly prohibited. You must incorporate actual text and data relevant to your specific service to ensure a realistic user experience. o Functional User Flow: The most critical objective is to implement a logical and functional user journey . Ensure that navigating through the app feels intuitive and realistic. Evaluation criteria Attendance Assignment (Mon) Assignment (Wed) Final Report Total 20% 20% 30% 30% 100% Evaluation Method 1. Grading System Your grade in this course will be determined by an absolute grading system, based on your attendance, weekly assignments, and a final project. 2. Attendance Attendance Check Mondays: Attendance is confirmed by your participation in the online quiz. Wednesdays: Attendance will be checked electronically. Please use the Kingo app or a similar application to tag your phone directly on the electronic attendance devices located at the front and back of the classroom. Absence Policy If you anticipate an absence, you must notify your instructor in advance and submit supporting documentation. You will automatically receive an F if you miss more than one - third (1/3) of all class sessions, regardless of the reason. Absences due to interns hips or jobs must also be reported in advance with official documentation

This assignment focuses on structural integrity and user experience (UX) logic rather than high-end visual aesthetics. o Detailed Guidelines: o Focus on Structure over Visual Polish: High-resolution images or complex graphic effects are not mandatory. However, even with a minimal use of color and imagery, the positioning of elements and information hierarchy must be refined enough to feel like a professional, real -world service. o Reflect Brand Identity: The prototype should clearly convey the brand’s character and concept through its overall tone, manner, and design choices. o Use Real Content: The use of 'Lorem Ipsum' or placeholder text is strictly prohibited. You must incorporate actual text and data relevant to your specific service to ensure a realistic user experience. o Functional User Flow: The most critical objective is to implement a logical and functional user journey . Ensure that navigating through the app feels intuitive and realistic. Evaluation criteria Attendance Assignment (Mon) Assignment (Wed) Final Report Total 20% 20% 30% 30% 100% Evaluation Method 1. 수업 비고: 1. Attendance
Two points will be deducted from the total attendance score of 10 points for each unexcused absence. Three instances of tardiness will be counted as one absence. Arrival 5–15 minutes after the start of class will be recorded as tardy, while arrival more than 15 minutes late will be recorded as an absence.

In accordance with university regulations, students must attend at least three-quarters of the total class hours to receive a final grade. Students with four or more unexcused absences will receive an F.

2. Assignments
Assignments will include critical reviews of research on artificial intelligence and visual communication, methodological exercises, and an individual research project.

3. Final Examination
The final examination will assess students’ understanding of key theories, concepts, research methods, and empirical findings related to artificial intelligence and visual communication.

4. Class Participation
Class participation will be evaluated based on students’ preparation for and active engagement in weekly discussions of assigned research articles.

5. Presentations
Presentation performance will be evaluated based on weekly presentations of assigned research articles and a final presentation of the student’s research proposal.

Course Objectives • recognise the welfare state not as a distant or abstract entity, but as an institutional environment that shapes the life chances, risks, responsibilities, and choices of students and their families, and as something that can be collectively debated and changed; • examine the historical origins and development of modern welfare states; • compare different welfare regimes and understand their institutional logics; • learn and accurately explain major theories of welfare state development; • critically examine contemporary welfare state debates, including non -standard work, welfare dualisation, basic income, welfare pluralism, and AI. 2 Weekly Schedule Week Weekly Topic Key Concepts 1 Why study the welfare state? Welfare state; social risk; social policy 2 Historical origins of the welfare state Poor Laws; social insurance; social rights; post-war welfare state 3 Theories of welfare state development 1 Industrialisation theory; modernisation theory; power resources theory 4 Theories of welfare state development 2 Interest group theory; state- centred theory; varieties of capitalism 5 Welfare regimes and comparative welfare states Welfare regimes; decommodification; stratification; familialism 6 Welfare politics as conflict over redistribution and deservingness Universalism and selectivism; deservingness; tax politics; welfare framing 7 Mid-term examination Mid-term examination 8 The development of the Korean welfare state Developmental state; familialism; democratisation 9 What kind of welfare state is Korea? Low-tax and low-welfare state; welfare dualisation; regressive welfare state 10 Crisis of the welfare state 1: traditional critiques of the welfare state Libertarian critique; liberal critique; neo-Marxist critique 11 Crisis of the welfare state 2: changes in industry and the labour market Deindustrialisation; labour market dualisation; automation; AI; skills mismatch 12 Public Claim Audit Workshop: From a Claim to an Argument 13 Crisis of the welfare state 3: demographic change, fiscal pressure, and social insurance Population ageing; fiscal sustainability; social insurance; intergenerational conflict 14 Responses to welfare state crises 1: welfare mix and the expansion of private responsibility Welfare mix; privatisation; corporate welfare; occupational welfare; third sector 3 Week Weekly Topic Key Concepts 15 Responses to welfare state crises 2: alternative models of income security, including basic income Universal basic income; negative income tax; basic assets; employment-based social protection; income security reform 16 Final examination and course synthesis Final examination Assignments The assignments are designed to help students connect welfare state theories to their own lives and households and to critically evaluate familiar public claims using course concepts and evidence. Detailed instructions, examples, and source guidance will be provided in class. The core requirements and grading weights stated below will remain fixed. 1. One Risk, Two Scenarios: “The Welfare State and Me” (10%) Students will choose one social risk or major life transition that could affect them directly or affect a family or household member whose income, care needs, or living arrangements are materially connected to their own. Examples may include unemployment, illness, disability, childbirth, care needs, housing insecurity, or retirement. Students will examine who would provide support and who would bear the costs in money, time, and care during the initial stage of the risk. They will then change one important condition - such as employment status, income, family support, gender, housing, or citizenship - and compare how the pattern of protection and vulnerability would change. An initial support map will be prepared during an in-class workshop and attached to the final report. The map is required but will not be graded separately; the full 10% assignment grade will be based on the final report. The report should consider the relevant roles of the state, family, employers, markets, civil society, and individuals, but students are not required to discuss every actor. The report must apply at least two course concepts and use at least one course reading and one relevant institutional or policy source. Students may alter personal details or use a fictional or composite case. Initial support map: Week 3 (required but ungraded) Final report: Week 5 Length: 2-3 A4 pages, excluding the initial map and

detail.CLASS_INFO:
***상세한 강의계획서는 개강에 맞추어 I-Campus의 공지란에 올려질 예정입니다. 출력하여 수업 첫시간에 지참합니다. 변동사항이 있으니 꼭 지참 바랍니다.***
이 과목은플립러닝(Flipped Learning) 강의이다. 화요일 10:30~11:45(75분)는 강의실에서의 실시간 대면수업으로, 그 외 시간은 온라인수업(75분)으로 구성한다. 대면수업은 Q&A 및 토론발표로 진행하며, 온라인수업은 주차별 주제에 대한 교수의 강의로 진행한다. 특정주차의 경우 대면수업과 온라인수업의 비중은 달라질 수 있다. 해당 주차의 강의시간 및 강의방법은 따로 공지한다.
detail.BIGO: 이 과목의 평가구성요소와 요소별 비중은 과제 20%, 팀프로젝트 30% 토론 및 발표 20%, 기말고사 30%로 한다. 출석은 1회 지각에 1점, 1회 무단결석에 2점씩 삭감하며, 4회 이상 무단결석은 과락으로 처리한다.

현재2026-2 해당 분반의 자체 전체16주 운영표와 학교 네이티브 수업시각·강의실에 따른 정규 대면 예약입니다. 실제 출석·시험·미확정 보강 시각은 확정하지 않았습니다. 제외 주차 16는 원문 시험/휴강/보강·자율학습/개별상담 또는 날짜충돌 구간입니다. 학교 공식8/31 시작의 7일 단위 주차 대응은 예약 제외 경계이며 실제 시험 날짜라는 주장이 아닙니다. 사전영상·휴일 온라인 보강·별도 현장/상담/과제 등 미확정 운영조건은 원문 그대로 보존하며 대면 예약으로 생성하지 않습니다. 각강좌 자체 사전영상/고정 대면구간 또는 오프라인 강좌구분을 확인했습니다. 단일1.5OFF 또는3hOFF native구간은 원문HH 그대로 사용하며 사전제작영상은 주간예약으로 생성하지 않습니다.

publishedEducationalOperatingTableSectio: Course outline This course investigates how gender is imbued with power. It will cover topics such as concept of gender and sexuality, the nature of masculinity and patriarchy, the coloniality of gender, and the epistemic implications of studying society from the perspective of women. The course focuses on theory but also includes specific case studies of gender-related issues in Korea and elsewhere. Through this course, students will 1) acquire social scientific knowledge about gender and power, in addition to 2) practicing academic communication in various formats. No prior knowledge is required from students. However, intellectual curiosity, analytical reasoning, and the ability to read social scientific articles in English are traits that would help you make most out of this course. The course instructor is committed to creating an environment open to all ideas, and students are encouraged to actively share their thoughts, including criticisms of the course content. Attendance does not by itself count towards the final grade, so students do not have to worry about the online attendance checks. However, noticeably frequent absence from class will compromise your attitude score, and you will not be able to register any points for the in-class quiz in those weeks that you decide to skip. Evaluation Evaluation category Percentage of final grade Notes Midterm 35% Open-book exam. Students are asked to write short essay-format exams. Students may write in English or Korean. Final 35% Open-book exam. Students are asked to write short essay-format exams. Students may write in English or Korean. In-class presentation 20% Students will need to do their presentations without reading from a script. This is to prevent the practice of mindlessly reciting what AI has made for you. Unlike the midterm and final, for which students may use English OR Korean, the presentation must be given in English. In-class quizzes 5% Short online interactive quizzes on Kahoot during offline tutorials (normally 5-7 questions). TWO lowest scores will be dropped from the semester average. Attitude 5% Students will by default get a full score. Noticeably frequent absences, breaking rules, disruptive acts, and other objectionable behavior will compromise the attitude score. Language policy The language of instruction is English, and the course instructor will speak English most of the time. Virtually all course material is in English. Students are encouraged to speak and write in English, but English-language proficiency will not directly affect your grades as long as you can express your ideas clearly. You may write in Korean for the midterm and final. Note that the presentation must be given in English. About the use of AI AI has become a part of life. Students may use AI as a tool for learning. Students may also use AI to help prepare in-class presentations. However, all material submitted for evaluation (incl. presentations) is expected to come from your own research and your own understanding of the course material. Merely reciting what AI has made for you without having studied / understood / digested the content is insufficient for a passing grade. At any point, the course instructor reserves the right to check whether a student has actually understood the content of his or her presentations or exam answers. Readings There is no required textbook for this course. There are no mandatory readings for this course. Optional

1) acquire social scientific knowledge about gender and power, in addition to 2) practicing academic communication in various formats. No prior knowledge is required from students. However, intellectual curiosity, analytical reasoning, and the ability to read social scientific articles in English are traits that would help you make most out of this course. The course instructor is committed to creating an environment open to all ideas, and students are encouraged to actively share their thoughts, including criticisms of the course content. Attendance does not by itself count towards the final grade, so students do not have to worry about the online attendance checks. However, noticeably frequent absence from class will compromise your attitude score, and you will not be able to register any points for the in-class quiz in those weeks that you decide to skip. Evaluation Evaluation category Percentage of final grade Notes Midterm 35% Open-book exam. Students are asked to write short essay-format exams. Students may write in English or Korean. Final 35% Open-book exam. Students are asked to write short essay-format exams. Students may write in English or Korean. In-class presentation 20% Students will need to do their presentations without reading from a script. This is to prevent the practice of mindlessly reciting what AI has made for you. Unlike the midterm and final, for which students may use English OR Korean, the presentation must be given in English. In-class quizzes 5% Short online interactive quizzes on Kahoot during offline tutorials (normally 5-7 questions). TWO lowest scores will be dropped from the semester average. Attitude 5% Students will by default get a full score. Noticeably frequent absences, breaking rules, disruptive acts, and other objectionable behavior will compromise the attitude score. Language policy The language of instruction is English, and the course instructor will speak English most of the time. Virtually all course material is in English. Students are encouraged to speak and write in English, but English-language proficiency will not directly affect your grades as long as you can express your ideas clearly. You may write in Korean for the midterm and final. Note that the presentation must be given in English. About the use of AI AI has become a part of life. Students may use AI as a tool for learning. Students may also use AI to help prepare in-class presentations. However, all material submitted for evaluation (incl. presentations) is expected to come from your own research and your own understanding of the course material. Merely reciting what AI has made for you without having studied / understood / digested the content is insufficient for a passing grade. At any point, the course instructor reserves the right to check whether a student has actually understood the content of his or her presentations or exam answers. Readings There is no required textbook for this course. There are no mandatory readings for this course. Optional references will be included at the end of every PPT deck. publishedEducationalOperatingTableSectio: Week 1 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (1) Global market / Globalization [Orientation] Give a brief overview of the syllabus. Ask any questions you may have by email or iCampus message. As the list of students will be finalized by the second week, class discussion groups will be announced then on iCampus. [Introduction] Introduce the concept of the global market, which will be studied during the semester, and examine why it is important to learn about and explore it. By providing a basic introduction, students will be able to answer the following questions after the first week of class: - What is the global market? - How has globalization affected global consumer culture in recent times? - Why do we need to keep an eye on the global market? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 1. Consumer Behavior Across Cultures Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 1. Globalization Imperative Week 2 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (2) Global consumer culture / Universalism / Cross-cultural consumer behavior [Main Contents & Questions] Learn about universalism in the global marketplace, while looking at cross-cultural consumer behavior. We will examine the universal characteristics of consumer markets and explore the implications of ‘universality’ in an unprecedentedly connected global age. Despite the interconnectedness of the world as a single marketplace, different cultures still have their own distinctive characteristics, resulting in differentiated consumer behavior. By the end of this week’s lecture, students will be able to answer the following questions: - What is universalism in the global market? - How does consumer behavior vary by culture? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 1. Consumer Behavior Across Cultures Week 3 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (3) Global consumer culture / Values / Norms / Comparative culture [Main Contents & Questions] Learn what values and norms are and how they exist in the context of culture. Students will learn about some of the most commonly discussed cultural distinctions in the literature and explore how values and norms vary across these distinctions. Students will learn about comparative cultural studies and use it to discuss real-life examples in class. By the end of the week, students should be able to answer the following questions: - What are values and norms and how do they relate to culture? - How does consumer behavior differ across cultures in the global marketplace according to comparative cultural studies? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 2. Values and Cultures Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 4. Global Cultural Environment and Buying Behavior Week 4 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (4) Global consumer culture / Convergence and divergence in consumer behavior [Main Contents & Questions] Learn about the various factors that influence consumer behavior in the global marketplace. Externally influenced by a variety of factors, consumer behavior can converge or diverge in different directions. We will explore the characteristics of these consumer cultures and apply them through discussion of real-world examples. By the end of the week, students will be able to answer the following questions: - What factors influence consumer behavior in the global market? - What are the characteristics of consumer cultures in the global market? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 3. Convergence and Divergence in Consumer Behavior Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 4. Global Cultural Environment and Buying Behavior Week 5 - Economic aspects of the global market (1) Economic background of global market expansion [Main Contents & Questions] Learn the fundamentals of why the global market is essential in terms of market structure. Students will explore the structural background to economic flows, including domestic market saturation, emerging markets, and the forces of global competition and cooperation. Based on their learning, students will discuss why global markets have become more expansive in the modern era, deepening their understanding of the economic structures of global markets and their impact on consumers. By the end of this weekly lesson, students will be able to answer the following questions: - Why are global markets essential in terms of market structure, and what are the key factors driving their expansion? - In what ways do global competition and cooperation influence consumer behavior and economic flows in globalized markets? [Reading] Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 1. Globalization Imperative Week 6 - Economic aspects of the global market (2) International macroeconomics / International economic indicators / Global market structure [Main Contents & Questions] Take an in-depth look at the economic organization of global consumer markets. Students will learn about various international macroeconomic indicators, such as GDP, PPP, and CPI, to understand how these metrics reflect the size and dynamics of global consumer markets. Students will then study the structure of competition in global markets by examining the distribution of human and technological resources and national competitiveness in global markets at a qualitative level. Through discussion, students will deepen their understanding of the qualitative and quantitative economic structure of global consumer markets by discussing the resources and various economic indicators that affect competitiveness in contemporary global marketplace. By the end of the week, students will be able to answer questions such as: - How do GDP, PPP and CPI provide insights into the economic strength of global consumer markets? - What are the key components of the economic structure of global consumer markets, and how do they influence consumer behavior? [Reading] Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 2. Economic Environment Week 7 - Economic aspects of the global market (3) Developed and Emerging markets [Main Contents & Questions] Examine the economic size and economic relationships of developed and emerging economies in the global consumer marketplace. Compare the differences in economic contexts and how these two classes of countries participate in global markets today. In addition, students will examine real-world examples to understand how global companies shape consumer markets in developed and emerging economies and influence consumer behavior. Through discussion, students will independently investigate real-world cases and apply their learning. By the end of this week, students will be able to answer the following question: - How do developed and emerging economies engage differently in global consumer markets in terms of market structure and consumer impact? [Reading] OECD, (2024.10.25.). How Shein Built a $66B Fast-Fashion Empire | WSJ The Economics Of, Available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gWotBPtsulo&t=406s Week 9 - Foundation of the global marketplace (1) Digital transformation / Digital consumer trends [Main Contents & Questions] Explore the digital landscape and the consumer trends within it that have made global markets more interconnected than ever before. Students will learn about consumer experiences and trends in social commerce, omni-channel and artificial intelligence, and apply them to real-world examples through discussion. By the end of the week, students will be able to answer questions such as: - How has digital technology affected global consumer trends? - What are the consumer trends in global markets driven by digital experiences? Week 10 - Foundation of the global marketplace (2) Global retail chains / Climate crisis [Main Contents & Questions] The retail structure of the global market is the focus this week. Students will learn about how the world is now organized as a marketplace, the interconnected structures that distribute goods to consumers, and apply the theory by looking at real world examples. Through discussion, students will share their own real-life consumer behaviors to shed light on the supply chain behind these purchases. In addition, the viewing material (documentary) will provide an opportunity to critically examine the environmental and socio-economic implications of the current global market structure and consider ways in which it could be improved. This will lead to a critique of the problems with global markets that will be discussed over the next few weeks. By the end of this week, students should be able to answer the following question: - How is the distribution structure of the global market organized? - What are the problems with the current distribution structure of the global market? 1) Global market / Globalization [Orientation] Give a brief overview of the syllabus. Ask any questions you may have by email or iCampus message. As the list of students will be finalized by the second week, class discussion groups will be announced then on iCampus. [Introduction] Introduce the concept of the global market, which will be studied during the semester, and examine why it is important to learn about and explore it. By providing a basic introduction, students will be able to answer the following questions after the first week of class: - What is the global market? - How has globalization affected global consumer culture in recent times? - Why do we need to keep an eye on the global market? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 1. Consumer Behavior Across Cultures Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 1. Globalization Imperative Week 2 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (2) Global consumer culture / Universalism / Cross-cultural consumer behavior [Main Contents & Questions] Learn about universalism in the global marketplace, while looking at cross-cultural consumer behavior. We will examine the universal characteristics of consumer markets and explore the implications of ‘universality’ in an unprecedentedly connected global age. Despite the interconnectedness of the world as a single marketplace, different cultures still have their own distinctive characteristics, resulting in differentiated consumer behavior. By the end of this week’s lecture, students will be able to answer the following questions: - What is universalism in the global market? - How does consumer behavior vary by culture? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 1. Consumer Behavior Across Cultures Week 3 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (3) Global consumer culture / Values / Norms / Comparative culture [Main Contents & Questions] Learn what values and norms are and how they exist in the context of culture. Students will learn about some of the most commonly discussed cultural distinctions in the literature and explore how values and norms vary across these distinctions. Students will learn about comparative cultural studies and use it to discuss real-life examples in class. By the end of the week, students should be able to answer the following questions: - What are values and norms and how do they relate to culture? - How does consumer behavior differ across cultures in the global marketplace according to comparative cultural studies? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 2. Values and Cultures Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 4. Global Cultural Environment and Buying Behavior Week 4 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (4) Global consumer culture / Convergence and divergence in consumer behavior [Main Contents & Questions] Learn about the various factors that influence consumer behavior in the global marketplace. Externally influenced by a variety of factors, consumer behavior can converge or diverge in different directions. We will explore the characteristics of these consumer cultures and apply them through discussion of real-world examples. By the end of the week, students will be able to answer the following questions: - What factors influence consumer behavior in the global market? - What are the characteristics of consumer cultures in the global market? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 3. Convergence and Divergence in Consumer Behavior Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 4. Global Cultural Environment and Buying Behavior Week 5 - Economic aspects of the global market (1) Economic background of global market expansion [Main Contents & Questions] Learn the fundamentals of why the global market is essential in terms of market structure. Students will explore the structural background to economic flows, including domestic market saturation, emerging markets, and the forces of global competition and cooperation. Based on their learning, students will discuss why global markets have become more expansive in the modern era, deepening their understanding of the economic structures of global markets and their impact on consumers. By the end of this weekly lesson, students will be able to answer the following questions: - Why are global markets essential in terms of market structure, and what are the key factors driving their expansion? - In what ways do global competition and cooperation influence consumer behavior and economic flows in globalized markets? [Reading] Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 1. Globalization Imperative Week 6 - Economic aspects of the global market (2) International macroeconomics / International economic indicators / Global market structure [Main Contents & Questions] Take an in-depth look at the economic organization of global consumer markets. Students will learn about various international macroeconomic indicators, such as GDP, PPP, and CPI, to understand how these metrics reflect the size and dynamics of global consumer markets. Students will then study the structure of competition in global markets by examining the distribution of human and technological resources and national competitiveness in global markets at a qualitative level. Through discussion, students will deepen their understanding of the qualitative and quantitative economic structure of global consumer markets by discussing the resources and various economic indicators that affect competitiveness in contemporary global marketplace. By the end of the week, students will be able to answer questions such as: - How do GDP, PPP and CPI provide insights into the economic strength of global consumer markets? - What are the key components of the economic structure of global consumer markets, and how do they influence consumer behavior? [Reading] Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 2. Economic Environment Week 7 - Economic aspects of the global market (3) Developed and Emerging markets [Main Contents & Questions] Examine the economic size and economic relationships of developed and emerging economies in the global consumer marketplace. Compare the differences in economic contexts and how these two classes of countries participate in global markets today. In addition, students will examine real-world examples to understand how global companies shape consumer markets in developed and emerging economies and influence consumer behavior. Through discussion, students will independently investigate real-world cases and apply their learning. By the end of this week, students will be able to answer the following question: - How do developed and emerging economies engage differently in global consumer markets in terms of market structure and consumer impact? [Reading] OECD, (2024.10.25.). 1) Digital transformation / Digital consumer trends [Main Contents & Questions] Explore the digital landscape and the consumer trends within it that have made global markets more interconnected than ever before. Students will learn about consumer experiences and trends in social commerce, omni-channel and artificial intelligence, and apply them to real-world examples through discussion. Week 10 - Foundation of the global marketplace (2) Global retail chains / Climate crisis [Main Contents & Questions] The retail structure of the global market is the focus this week. Students will learn about how the world is now organized as a marketplace, the interconnected structures that distribute goods to consumers, and apply the theory by looking at real world examples. Through discussion, students will share their own real-life consumer behaviors to shed light on the supply chain behind these purchases. In addition, the viewing material (documentary) will provide an opportunity to critically examine the environmental and socio-economic implications of the current global market structure and consider ways in which it could be improved. This will lead to a critique of the problems with global markets that will be discussed over the next few weeks. By the end of this week, students should be able to answer the following question: - How is the distribution structure of the global market organized? - What are the problems with the current distribution structure of the global market? Ask any questions you may have by email or iCampus message. As the list of students will be finalized by the second week, class discussion groups will be announced then on iCampus. [Introduction] Introduce the concept of the global market, which will be studied during the semester, and examine why it is important to learn about and explore it. By providing a basic introduction, students will be able to answer the following questions after the first week of class: - What is the global market? - How has globalization affected global consumer culture in recent times? - Why do we need to keep an eye on the global market? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 1. Consumer Behavior Across Cultures Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 1. Globalization Imperative Week 2 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (2) Global consumer culture / Universalism / Cross-cultural consumer behavior [Main Contents & Questions] Learn about universalism in the global marketplace, while looking at cross-cultural consumer behavior. We will examine the universal characteristics of consumer markets and explore the implications of ‘universality’ in an unprecedentedly connected global age. Despite the interconnectedness of the world as a single marketplace, different cultures still have their own distinctive characteristics, resulting in differentiated consumer behavior. By the end of this week’s lecture, students will be able to answer the following questions: - What is universalism in the global market? - How does consumer behavior vary by culture? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 1. Consumer Behavior Across Cultures Week 3 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (3) Global consumer culture / Values / Norms / Comparative culture [Main Contents & Questions] Learn what values and norms are and how they exist in the context of culture. Students will learn about some of the most commonly discussed cultural distinctions in the literature and explore how values and norms vary across these distinctions. Students will learn about comparative cultural studies and use it to discuss real-life examples in class. By the end of the week, students should be able to answer the following questions: - What are values and norms and how do they relate to culture? - How does consumer behavior differ across cultures in the global marketplace according to comparative cultural studies? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 2. Values and Cultures Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 4. Global Cultural Environment and Buying Behavior Week 4 - Sociocultural aspects of the global market (4) Global consumer culture / Convergence and divergence in consumer behavior [Main Contents & Questions] Learn about the various factors that influence consumer behavior in the global marketplace. Externally influenced by a variety of factors, consumer behavior can converge or diverge in different directions. We will explore the characteristics of these consumer cultures and apply them through discussion of real-world examples. By the end of the week, students will be able to answer the following questions: - What factors influence consumer behavior in the global market? - What are the characteristics of consumer cultures in the global market? [Readings] De Mooij, & Marieke K. (2019). Consumer Behavior and Culture: Consequences for Global Marketing and Advertising, Chapter 3. Convergence and Divergence in Consumer Behavior Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 4. Global Cultural Environment and Buying Behavior Week 5 - Economic aspects of the global market (1) Economic background of global market expansion [Main Contents & Questions] Learn the fundamentals of why the global market is essential in terms of market structure. Students will explore the structural background to economic flows, including domestic market saturation, emerging markets, and the forces of global competition and cooperation. Based on their learning, students will discuss why global markets have become more expansive in the modern era, deepening their understanding of the economic structures of global markets and their impact on consumers. By the end of this weekly lesson, students will be able to answer the following questions: - Why are global markets essential in terms of market structure, and what are the key factors driving their expansion? - In what ways do global competition and cooperation influence consumer behavior and economic flows in globalized markets? [Reading] Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 1. Globalization Imperative Week 6 - Economic aspects of the global market (2) International macroeconomics / International economic indicators / Global market structure [Main Contents & Questions] Take an in-depth look at the economic organization of global consumer markets. Students will learn about various international macroeconomic indicators, such as GDP, PPP, and CPI, to understand how these metrics reflect the size and dynamics of global consumer markets. Students will then study the structure of competition in global markets by examining the distribution of human and technological resources and national competitiveness in global markets at a qualitative level. Through discussion, students will deepen their understanding of the qualitative and quantitative economic structure of global consumer markets by discussing the resources and various economic indicators that affect competitiveness in contemporary global marketplace. By the end of the week, students will be able to answer questions such as: - How do GDP, PPP and CPI provide insights into the economic strength of global consumer markets? - What are the key components of the economic structure of global consumer markets, and how do they influence consumer behavior? [Reading] Masaaki Kotobe, & Kristiaan Helsen, (2020). Global Marketing Management, Chapter 2. Economic Environment Week 7 - Economic aspects of the global market (3) Developed and Emerging markets [Main Contents & Questions] Examine the economic size and economic relationships of developed and emerging economies in the global consumer marketplace. Compare the differences in economic contexts and how these two classes of countries participate in global markets today. In addition, students will examine real-world examples to understand how global companies shape consumer markets in developed and emerging economies and influence consumer behavior. Through discussion, students will independently investigate real-world cases and apply their learning. By the end of this week, students will be able to answer the following question: - How do developed and emerging economies engage differently in global consumer markets in terms of market structure and consumer impact? [Reading] OECD, (2024.10.25.). How Shein Built a $66B Fast-Fashion Empire | WSJ The Economics Of, Available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gWotBPtsulo&t=406s Week 9 - Foundation of the global marketplace (1) Digital transformation / Digital consumer trends [Main Contents & Questions] Explore the digital landscape and the consumer trends within it that have made global markets more interconnected than ever before. Students will learn about consumer experiences and trends in social commerce, omni-channel and artificial intelligence, and apply them to real-world examples through discussion. By the end of the week, students will be able to answer questions such as: - How has digital technology affected global consumer trends? - What are the consumer trends in global markets driven by digital experiences? The Impact Of Digital Transformation On Retail Management And Consumer Behavior. IOSR Journal of Business and Management (IOSR-JBM) e-ISSN, 06-14. Week 10 - Foundation of the global marketplace (2) Global retail chains / Climate crisis [Main Contents & Questions] The retail structure of the global market is the focus this week. Students will learn about how the world is now organized as a marketplace, the interconnected structures that distribute goods to consumers, and apply the theory by looking at real world examples. Through discussion, students will share their own real-life consumer behaviors to shed light on the supply chain behind these purchases. In addition, the viewing material (documentary) will provide an opportunity to critically examine the environmental and socio-economic implications of the current global market structure and consider ways in which it could be improved. This will lead to a critique of the problems with global markets that will be discussed over the next few weeks. By the end of this week, students should be able to answer the following question: - How is the distribution structure of the global market organized? - What are the problems with the current distribution structure of the global market? Students will learn about globalization and localization by examining and comparing examples of companies in today’s global marketplace. Students will also develop a critical awareness by learning about acculturation and cultural homogenization and why they can be problematic. Students will broaden their horizons by researching and sharing real-life examples of acculturation and cultural homogenization issues in the global marketplace. After this week’s lectures, students will be able to answer the following questions: - What are globalization/localization/acculturation/cultural homogenization and how do they differ? - Why can acculturation and cultural homogenization be problematic in the global marketplace? Based on their learning, students will discuss why global markets have become more expansive in the modern era, deepening their understanding of the economic structures of global markets and their impact on consumers. Students will learn about various international macroeconomic indicators, such as GDP, PPP, and CPI, to understand how these metrics reflect the size and dynamics of global consumer markets. Ask any questions you may have by email or iCampus message. As the list of students will be finalized by the second week, class discussion groups will be announced then on iCampus. [Introduction] Introduce the concept of the global market, which will be studied during the semester, and examine why it is important to learn about and explore it.
